topics.title: How do we analyse the chemicals in living tissue?

learn.hook: Carbon is a tiny 0.03% of the Earth's crust, but about 18.5% of your body. Life is a carbon-hungry chemist.
points: Grind a living tissue in trichloroacetic acid (Cl₃CCOOH) with a mortar and pestle to get a slurry. Strain it through cheesecloth or cotton to get two fractions: the filtrate (acid-soluble pool) and the retentate (acid-insoluble fraction).
Analytical techniques applied to separated compounds give their molecular formula and probable structure. All carbon compounds obtained from living tissues are called biomolecules.

Ash analysis: weigh the tissue (wet weight), dry it to remove water (dry weight), then burn it completely. Carbon compounds are oxidised to gases (CO₂, water vapour) and removed; the remaining ash contains inorganic elements such as calcium and magnesium.
Inorganic compounds such as sulphate and phosphate are also seen in the acid-soluble fraction.

Living matter is far richer in carbon (18.5% vs 0.03%), hydrogen (0.5% vs 0.14%), oxygen (65.0% vs 46.6%) and nitrogen (3.3% vs very little) than the Earth's crust, but much poorer in silicon (negligible vs 27.7%).

example.q: Order the steps of ash analysis.
steps: Weigh the fresh tissue: wet weight.
Dry it to evaporate water: dry weight.
Burn it completely: carbon compounds leave as CO₂ and water vapour.
Weigh and analyse the remaining ash for inorganic elements.
example.answer: Wet weight → dry weight → burning → ash with inorganic elements

learn.reallife: Food testing labs under FSSAI measure ash content in spices and flours to check for adulteration with sand or chalk.

topics.title: Amino acids, sugars and nucleotides: the small building blocks

learn.hook: Only 20 kinds of amino acids build every protein in your body, from hair keratin to the enzymes in your saliva.
points: Amino acids have an amino group and a carboxyl group on the same carbon, the α-carbon; they are substituted methanes with four groups: hydrogen, carboxyl, amino and a variable R group. Twenty types occur in proteins.

R group: hydrogen in glycine, methyl in alanine, hydroxymethyl in serine. Amino acids may be acidic (glutamic acid), basic (lysine) or neutral (valine); aromatic ones are tyrosine, phenylalanine and tryptophan.
The –NH₂ and –COOH groups ionise, so the structure of an amino acid changes with pH; at a particular pH it exists as a zwitterion carrying both a positive and a negative charge.
Simple sugars (monosaccharides) such as glucose and ribose are carbohydrate units.

Nitrogen bases: adenine, guanine, cytosine, uracil, thymine. Base + sugar = nucleoside (adenosine, guanosine, thymidine, uridine, cytidine). Base + sugar + phosphate = nucleotide (adenylic, guanylic, thymidylic, uridylic, cytidylic acids).

example.q: Adenine is joined to a sugar, and a phosphate is then esterified to the sugar. Name the compound at each stage.
steps: Adenine + sugar = nucleoside: adenosine.
Adding a phosphate gives a nucleotide: adenylic acid.

learn.reallife: Dal and paneer in an Indian thali are rich sources of amino acids, the building blocks your body uses to make its own proteins.

topics.title: Lipids: fatty acids, glycerides and phospholipids

learn.hook: Why does coconut oil turn solid on a cold Delhi winter morning, but gingelly (til) oil stays liquid? Melting points tell the story.
points: Lipids are generally water-insoluble. A fatty acid has a carboxyl group attached to an R group, which may be methyl, ethyl or a chain of –CH₂ groups (1 to 19 carbons).
Palmitic acid has 16 carbons and arachidonic acid has 20 carbons, including the carboxyl carbon. Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bond; unsaturated ones have one or more.

Glycerol is trihydroxy propane. Fatty acids esterified with glycerol give monoglycerides, diglycerides and triglycerides. These are called fats or oils by melting point; oils (e.g. gingelly oil) have lower melting points and stay liquid in winter.
Phospholipids contain phosphorus and a phosphorylated organic compound; they are found in cell membranes, e.g. lecithin. Neural tissues have more complex lipids.
Lipids are small (below 800 Da) and are not true macromolecules. They appear in the acid-insoluble fraction because grinding breaks membranes into water-insoluble vesicles.

example.q: How many fatty acid molecules are esterified to one glycerol in a triglyceride?
steps: Glycerol has three –OH groups.
In a triglyceride, all three are esterified with fatty acids.

learn.reallife: India's National Institute of Nutrition advises using a mix of oils because different oils provide different proportions of saturated and unsaturated fatty acids.

games.title: Saturated or unsaturated?
items: One or more C=C double bonds

quiz.q: Glycerol is chemically:
quiz.explain: Glycerol has three hydroxyl groups on a propane backbone.

quiz.explain: Lecithin contains phosphorus and is found in membranes.

quiz.q: A fatty acid with one or more C=C double bonds is:
quiz.explain: Double bonds make a fatty acid unsaturated.

quiz.explain: Membrane fragments form vesicles that separate with the macromolecules.
options: They are polymers of amino acids

quiz.explain: Oils stay liquid at lower temperatures.

quiz.q: How many carbon atoms does arachidonic acid have?
quiz.explain: Arachidonic acid has 20 carbons including the carboxyl carbon.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

quiz.explain: Both true; their small size means they are not true macromolecules.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect molecular weight with the macromolecule category

teach.ask: Gappu sees coconut oil turn solid in winter. Explain fatty acids, glycerides and phospholipids to him!
teach.praise: Tweet! Fatty acids plus glycerol make fats and oils; phospholipids build membranes!
teach.nudge: Good! What is a triglyceride, and how do oils differ from fats?

learn.hook: The yellow of haldi, the bitterness of neem and the latex of rubber trees in Kerala are all 'extra' chemicals that plants did not need just to stay alive.
points: Primary metabolites, such as amino acids and sugars, have identifiable functions and known roles in normal physiological processes.
Secondary metabolites are found in plants, fungi and microbes. We do not yet understand the role of all of them in their hosts, but many are useful to humans and some have ecological importance.
Pigments: carotenoids, anthocyanins. Alkaloids: morphine, codeine. Terpenoids: monoterpenes, diterpenes. Essential oils: lemon grass oil.
Toxins: abrin, ricin. Lectins: concanavalin A. Drugs: vinblastine, curcumin. Polymeric substances: rubber, gums, cellulose.
Human uses include rubber, drugs, spices, scents and pigments.

example.q: Classify curcumin and ricin as secondary metabolites.
steps: Curcumin from turmeric is used as a drug: drug category.
Ricin from castor is poisonous: toxin category.
example.answer: Curcumin is a drug; ricin is a toxin.

learn.reallife: Kerala's rubber plantations, Assam's lemon grass and the turmeric of Erode in Tamil Nadu all trade in secondary metabolites.

quiz.explain: NCERT lists concanavalin A as a lectin.

quiz.explain: Amino acids have known roles in normal physiology.

quiz.q: Abrin and ricin are:
quiz.explain: They are poisonous secondary metabolites.

quiz.q: Carotenoids and anthocyanins are:
quiz.explain: They give colour.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Rubber is a secondary (polymeric) metabolite (A true). R is false: secondary metabolites do not have such a clearly known role in normal physiology.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If plants don't need haldi colour to live, why make it?' Explain primary and secondary metabolites!
teach.praise: Chirp! Primary keeps life running; secondary gives colour, defence and our medicines!
teach.nudge: Good! What is the difference between primary and secondary metabolites?

topics.title: Biomacromolecules and the composition of a cell

learn.hook: If you dried out a typical cell, most of what's left would be protein. But first, you'd have to remove a lot of water.
points: The acid-soluble pool contains molecules with molecular weights from about 18 to around 800 daltons (Da).

The acid-insoluble fraction contains four types of organic compounds: proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides and lipids. Except lipids, they have molecular weights of ten thousand daltons and above.
Biomolecules are micromolecules (molecular weight below 1000 Da) or macromolecules (biomacromolecules). Proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides are true macromolecules.
Average composition of cells: water 70 to 90%, proteins 10 to 15%, nucleic acids 5 to 7%, carbohydrates 3%, lipids 2%, ions 1%.
So water is the most abundant chemical in living organisms, followed by proteins.

example.q: Which is the second most abundant component of a cell after water?
steps: Water is 70 to 90%.
Proteins are 10 to 15%, higher than nucleic acids (5 to 7%), carbohydrates (3%) and lipids (2%).

learn.reallife: The water in your body is why doctors in Indian hospitals watch for dehydration so closely during summer heat waves.

quiz.q: Which is the most abundant chemical in living organisms?
quiz.explain: Water makes up 70 to 90% of cells.

quiz.q: Which compounds of the acid-insoluble fraction are NOT true macromolecules?
quiz.explain: Lipids are small but appear there because of membrane vesicles.

quiz.q: Micromolecules have molecular weights below about:
quiz.explain: Micromolecules are below 1000 daltons.

quiz.mistake: Gives the water or nucleic acid share

quiz.q: The acid-soluble pool contains molecules of molecular weight from about:
quiz.explain: Small molecules such as water (18 Da) to about 800 Da.

quiz.q: Carbohydrates make up what percentage of a cell, on average?
quiz.explain: NCERT gives 3% carbohydrates.

quiz.q: Which is a true biomacromolecule?
quiz.explain: DNA is a polymer with very high molecular weight.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides are found in the acid-soluble pool. Reason (R): These compounds have molecular weights of ten thousand daltons and above.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: these macromolecules are in the acid-insoluble fraction; the acid-soluble pool has molecules of about 18 to 800 Da. R is true: their very high molecular weight is why they stay in the acid-insoluble fraction.
quiz.mistake: Judges the assertion true just because the reason is a correct fact

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know what a cell is mostly made of. Explain micro- and macromolecules and the cell's composition!
teach.praise: Tweet! Mostly water, then proteins, with big macromolecules in the acid-insoluble part!
teach.nudge: Good! What is most abundant in cells, and which molecules are true macromolecules?

learn.hook: The most abundant protein on the whole planet is not in animals at all. It sits in every green leaf, fixing CO₂.
points: Proteins are polypeptides: linear chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
With 20 types of amino acids, a protein is a heteropolymer, not a homopolymer (which repeats a single type of monomer).
Essential amino acids must come from the diet; non-essential amino acids can be made by the body.

Functions: collagen (intercellular ground substance), trypsin (enzyme), insulin (hormone), antibody (fights infectious agents), receptor (sensory reception: smell, taste, hormone), GLUT-4 (glucose transport into cells). Some proteins transport nutrients across membranes.
Collagen is the most abundant protein in the animal world; RuBisCO (ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase) is the most abundant protein in the whole biosphere.

example.q: Why is a protein called a heteropolymer while cellulose is a homopolymer?
steps: A protein is built from up to 20 different amino acids.
Cellulose is built from only one monomer, glucose.
example.answer: Protein has many kinds of monomers; cellulose has only glucose.

learn.reallife: Pulses (dal) and milk are important in Indian diets partly because they supply essential amino acids the body cannot make.

learn.hook: Drop iodine on a slice of potato and it turns blue-black. Drop it on cotton wool and nothing happens. Both are chains of glucose. Why the difference?
points: Polysaccharides are long chains of sugars (monosaccharides) as building blocks.
Cellulose is a homopolymer of glucose. Starch (plant energy store) and glycogen (animal store) are other variants; inulin is a polymer of fructose.
In a chain such as glycogen, the right end is the reducing end and the left end the non-reducing end; glycogen is branched.
Starch forms helical secondary structures that can hold I₂ molecules, giving a blue colour. Cellulose has no complex helices, cannot hold iodine and gives no colour.

Plant cell walls are made of cellulose; paper and cotton fibre are cellulosic. Complex polysaccharides with amino sugars and modified sugars (e.g. glucosamine, N-acetyl galactosamine) include chitin in arthropod exoskeletons.

example.q: Why does iodine solution turn blue with starch but not with cellulose?
steps: Starch forms helices that can hold iodine molecules; starch-I₂ is blue.
Cellulose lacks complex helices and cannot hold iodine.
example.answer: Only starch's helices trap iodine to form a blue complex.

learn.reallife: School and FSSAI-style kitchen tests use iodine to detect starch added as an adulterant to milk or paneer: a blue colour gives it away.

learn.hook: Your entire genetic instruction book is written with just four letters, A, T, G and C, strung on a sugar-phosphate thread.
points: Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) are polynucleotides. With polysaccharides and polypeptides, they form the true macromolecular fraction of tissues.
A nucleotide has three chemically distinct parts: a heterocyclic nitrogen base, a monosaccharide (pentose sugar) and phosphoric acid (phosphate).
Bases: adenine, guanine, cytosine, uracil, thymine. Adenine and guanine are substituted purines; cytosine, uracil and thymine are substituted pyrimidines.
The sugar is ribose in RNA and 2'-deoxyribose in DNA.
Thymine occurs in DNA and uracil in RNA; adenine, guanine and cytosine occur in both.

example.q: Which of these bases are purines: adenine, cytosine, guanine, thymine, uracil?
steps: Purines have the purine double-ring skeleton.
Adenine and guanine are substituted purines; the rest are pyrimidines.

learn.reallife: DNA fingerprinting labs, such as the Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics in Hyderabad, read the sequence of these bases to identify people.

quiz.q: Which bases are purines?
quiz.explain: A and G are purines; C, T and U are pyrimidines.

quiz.q: The sugar present in DNA is:
quiz.explain: DNA contains deoxyribose; RNA contains ribose.

quiz.q: A nucleotide is made of:
quiz.explain: These three parts make a nucleotide.
quiz.mistake: Leaves out the sugar or phosphate
options: A nitrogen base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate
An amino acid and a sugar
Only a base and a phosphate

quiz.q: Which base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
quiz.explain: RNA has uracil in place of thymine.

quiz.q: Nucleic acids are polymers of:
quiz.explain: Nucleic acids are polynucleotides.

quiz.q: Cytosine is a:
quiz.explain: Cytosine is a pyrimidine.

quiz.q: How many types of nitrogen bases occur in nucleic acids in total (DNA and RNA together)?
quiz.explain: A, G, C, T and U.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): RNA contains ribose sugar. Reason (R): In RNA, thymine is replaced by uracil.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

quiz.explain: Both true facts about RNA, but having uracil does not explain why its sugar is ribose.
quiz.mistake: Treats two features of RNA as cause and effect

teach.ask: Gappu hears that DNA is 'written in four letters'. Explain nucleotides, purines and pyrimidines!
teach.praise: Chirp! Base, sugar, phosphate: two purines and three pyrimidines. Genetic alphabet learned!
teach.nudge: Good! What are the three parts of a nucleotide, and which bases are purines?

learn.hook: A protein is like a phone charger cable: first a sequence of wires, then twisted, then coiled into a ball, and sometimes several bundled together.
points: Primary structure: the sequence of amino acids, i.e. the positional information. The first amino acid is the N-terminal amino acid; the last is the C-terminal amino acid.
Secondary structure: the chain is not a rigid rod; some portions fold into a helix (only right-handed helices occur in proteins), and other regions fold into other forms.
Tertiary structure: the long chain folds upon itself like a hollow woollen ball, giving a 3-D shape. It is absolutely necessary for many biological activities of proteins.
Quaternary structure: the arrangement of two or more folded polypeptides (subunits) with respect to each other.
Adult human haemoglobin has 4 subunits: two α and two β.

example.q: Which structural level is shown by haemoglobin but not by a single-chain protein?
steps: A single chain can have primary, secondary and tertiary structure.
Haemoglobin has four subunits (2 α + 2 β) arranged together.
Arrangement of subunits is quaternary structure.

learn.reallife: Thalassaemia, common in parts of India, is linked to defects in the α or β chains of haemoglobin, a protein with quaternary structure.

topics.title: Enzymes and the speed of chemical reactions

learn.hook: Without an enzyme, about 200 molecules of carbonic acid form in an hour. With carbonic anhydrase, about 600,000 form every second.
points: Almost all enzymes are proteins; some nucleic acids act as enzymes, called ribozymes. In the tertiary structure, a crevice or pocket called the active site holds the substrate.

Inorganic catalysts work well at high temperature and pressure, but enzymes are damaged at high temperatures (say above 40°C). Enzymes from thermophilic organisms in hot vents and sulphur springs stay stable even at 80 to 90°C.
A physical change alters shape or state without breaking bonds (ice melting). A chemical reaction breaks and forms bonds, e.g. Ba(OH)₂ + H₂SO₄ → BaSO₄ + 2H₂O, or hydrolysis of starch to glucose.
Rate of reaction = amount of product formed per unit time. As a rule of thumb, the rate doubles or halves for every 10°C change. Carbonic anhydrase speeds CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ about 10 million times.

A metabolic pathway is a series of enzyme-catalysed steps. Glucose becomes pyruvic acid through ten enzyme-catalysed reactions; in skeletal muscle under anaerobic conditions lactic acid forms, and in yeast during fermentation ethanol forms.

example.q: A reaction at 25°C gives 100 units of product per minute. Using the 10°C rule of thumb, estimate the rate at 35°C.
steps: A 10°C rise roughly doubles the rate.
100 × 2 = 200 units per minute.

learn.reallife: Enzymes from heat-loving microbes are used in PCR machines in Indian diagnostic labs, which cycle up to about 95°C to test for infections.

games.title: Physical change or chemical reaction?
items: Change of shape without breaking bonds

Rate is 10 units at 10°C; rate at 30°C?

quiz.explain: Yeast makes ethanol; muscle under anaerobic conditions makes lactic acid.

topics.title: How enzymes work: ES complex, activation energy and the catalytic cycle

learn.hook: Rolling a heavy boulder over a hill takes a big push even if the other side is downhill. Enzymes dig a tunnel through that hill.
points: The substrate (S) binds the enzyme's active site to form a short-lived enzyme-substrate complex (ES), which is essential for catalysis: E + S ⇌ ES → EP → E + P.
The substrate is converted to product through an unstable, high-energy transition state.

If the product is at a lower energy level than the substrate, the reaction is exothermic and needs no heating; if higher, it is endothermic. Either way, the substrate must pass through the transition state.
Activation energy is the difference in energy between the substrate and the transition state. Enzymes lower this energy barrier, making S → P easier.

Catalytic cycle: (i) substrate binds the active site; (ii) binding induces the enzyme to change shape and fit more tightly (induced fit); (iii) the active site breaks bonds of the substrate and an enzyme-product complex forms; (iv) products are released, and the free enzyme is ready for another substrate.

example.q: In an energy diagram, the substrate is at 40 units, the transition state without enzyme at 100 units and with enzyme at 70 units. Find the activation energy with and without the enzyme.
steps: Without enzyme: 100 - 40 = 60 units.
With enzyme: 70 - 40 = 30 units.
The enzyme halves the barrier here.
example.answer: Without enzyme 60 units; with enzyme 30 units.

learn.reallife: Biological washing powders sold in India contain enzymes that lower activation energy so stains break down in cold water, saving electricity.

quiz.explain: Energy is released, so it is exothermic.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the activation energy barrier exists even for exothermic reactions, so enzymes help.
quiz.mistake: Thinks exothermic reactions need no help at all

topics.title: Factors affecting enzyme activity and inhibition

learn.hook: Why do we keep curd in the fridge and boil milk to stop it spoiling? Temperature controls enzymes.
points: Enzymes work in a narrow range of temperature and pH. Each has an optimum temperature and optimum pH where activity is highest; activity falls above and below the optimum.
Low temperature keeps an enzyme temporarily inactive; high temperature destroys activity because the protein is denatured by heat.
As substrate concentration rises, the reaction velocity first rises and then reaches a maximum, Vmax, which is not exceeded by adding more substrate, because all enzyme molecules are saturated.

A chemical that binds an enzyme and shuts off its activity is an inhibitor. A competitive inhibitor closely resembles the substrate and competes for the substrate-binding site, so the substrate cannot bind.
Example: malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase because it resembles succinate. Competitive inhibitors are often used to control bacterial pathogens.

example.q: An enzyme gives a velocity of 50 units at 2 mM substrate, 80 at 4 mM, 100 at 8 mM and 100 at 16 mM. What is Vmax and why does the curve level off?
steps: Velocity stops rising at 100 units.
All enzyme molecules are busy (saturated); extra substrate finds no free enzyme.
example.answer: Vmax = 100 units; the enzyme is saturated.

learn.reallife: Many antibiotics used in Indian hospitals work as enzyme inhibitors in bacteria; for example, sulpha drugs compete with a substrate bacteria need to make folic acid.

quiz.explain: They can block key bacterial enzymes.

teach.praise: Chirp! Heat denatures, cold pauses, Vmax caps the speed, and inhibitors block the active site!

learn.hook: Some enzymes can't work alone. They need a 'sidekick' such as zinc, haem or a vitamin-derived NAD.
points: Six classes: oxidoreductases/dehydrogenases (oxidation-reduction between two substrates), transferases (transfer of a group other than hydrogen, S–G + S' → S + S'–G), hydrolases (hydrolysis of ester, ether, peptide, glycosidic, C–C, C–halide or P–N bonds).

Lyases remove groups from substrates by mechanisms other than hydrolysis, leaving double bonds. Isomerases interconvert optical, geometric or positional isomers. Ligases link two compounds, joining C–O, C–S, C–N, P–O bonds and so on.
Many enzymes need non-protein co-factors to be active; the protein part is the apoenzyme. Removing the co-factor destroys catalytic activity.

Prosthetic groups are organic and tightly bound, e.g. haem in peroxidase and catalase (which break down H₂O₂ into water and oxygen). Co-enzymes are organic but bind only transiently and serve many enzymes; many contain vitamins, e.g. NAD and NADP contain niacin.
Metal ions form coordination bonds with the active site and substrate, e.g. zinc for carboxypeptidase.

example.q: An enzyme joins two molecules to form a C–N bond using energy. Which class is it?
steps: Joining two compounds by forming a bond is ligation.
So the enzyme is a ligase.

learn.reallife: Niacin (vitamin B3), present in groundnuts and whole grains common in Indian diets, is needed to make the co-enzymes NAD and NADP.
